name: Kaifeng
info: Kaifeng is a city on the southern bank of the Yellow River in east-central Henan, China, founded as the Wei capital Daliang in 361 BCE, later the Song capital Dongjing, and one of the Eight Ancient Capitals of China.

facts.founded: King Hui of Wei moved the Wei capital to Yi in 361 BCE and built the city of Daliang there; two older cities, Yi and Qifeng, already stood nearby in the Spring and Autumn period.
facts.where: On the southern bank of the Yellow River in east-central Henan province, China, east of the provincial capital Zhengzhou.
facts.known: The Wei capital Daliang; the Song capital Dongjing; the Iron Pagoda of 1049; Su Song's astronomical clock tower; the Jin court's move there in 1214; the flooding of 1642; the Kaifeng Jews
facts.today: Kaifeng is a prefecture-level city of Henan province, and the capital of the province until 1954.

t: Kaifeng began as the Wei capital Daliang in 361 BCE, was destroyed when Qin conquered Wei, and revived as a canal town, Junyi, Bianzhou and then the capital of four of the Five Dynasties.

Under the Song dynasty, which made it its capital in 960, Dongjing became the largest and most prosperous city in China, and it is believed to have been the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127.
Jin forces took it in 1127 and Mongol forces in 1233, and the Yellow River flooded it repeatedly, most destructively in 1642, after which only 30,000 of its 370,000 people remained.
dyk: The astronomical clock tower of Su Song at Dongjing was crowned with a water-powered armillary sphere and incorporated an escapement mechanism two hundred years before escapements were found in the clockworks of Europe.
ev: King Hui of Wei builds the city of Daliang
Cao Cao repairs the Suiyang Canal at Junyi, opening the Bian River to the Yangtze and Huaihe
Li Mian builds a new city wall at Bianzhou
The Song dynasty makes the city its capital
Jin forces occupy Dongjing and take the Song imperial family north
The city falls to Mongol forces after a siege of ten months
The Ming army floods the city with the Yellow River to drown besieging rebels
The capital of Henan province moves to Zhengzhou

sections.origins:
Kaifeng lies on the southern bank of the Yellow River in east-central Henan. In the Spring and Autumn period two ancient cities stood in its vicinity: Yi, built by the state of Wey, and Qifeng, built by Duke Zhuang of Zheng south of the present-day city. Wey was later annexed by the state of Wei.

In the Warring States period the lords of Wei held the title of King of Liang. In 361 BCE King Hui of Wei moved the Wei capital from the city of An to Yi and built the city of Daliang there, after which the state of Wei was called Liang. The first of many canals in the area, linking a local river to the Yellow River, was built in this period. When Qin conquered Wei, Daliang was destroyed and abandoned except for a mid-sized market town, which was renamed Junyi.

Qifeng was renamed Kaifeng after the Qin conquest of China. Its original name was Qifeng, and the syllable qi was changed to the essentially synonymous kai to avoid the naming taboo of Liu Qi, Emperor Jing of Han. The old city of Qifeng later declined and was abandoned, and its ruins lie near the present-day town of Zhuxian.
sections.growth:
Under the Han dynasty Junyi was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang, ruled by Liu Wu, a son of the Han emperor Wen, as Prince of Liang. Liu Wu restored the old city walls and put up many buildings, and Daliang became a centre of music and art, a refuge for artists and a city of splendid gardens, although it was of little political importance at this period. In 202 Cao Cao repaired the Suiyang Canal at Junyi, opening the Bian River to the Yangtze and Huaihe rivers. The canal allowed grain to be carried north from those regions, and Junyi, at a junction of waterway and land routes, recovered economically.

Early in the 7th century the old Daliang, now called Bianzhou, became a major commercial hub when it was connected to the Grand Canal and to a canal running to western Shandong. In 955 Emperor Shizong of Zhou mobilised 100,000 civilians to build an outer city.

Dongjing reached its peak in the 11th century as a commercial and industrial centre at the intersection of four major canals. It was then surrounded by three rings of walls and probably had a population of between 600,000 and 700,000. It is believed to have been the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127. Another figure puts the population at over 400,000, living both inside and outside the wall.
sections.rulers:
The city was the capital of the Wei state from 361 BCE, until Qin conquered Wei. Under the Han dynasty it was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang. In the Eastern Han the kingdom became Liang County, and part of it became the Chenliu Commandery, which was re-established as a principality under Cao Wei and the Jin dynasty. In 534 Emperor Xiaojing of Eastern Wei changed Chenliu County to Liangzhou, and under the Northern Zhou it was renamed Bianzhou after the Bian River. In 781, under the Tang, its governor Li Mian built a new city wall 22 li in circumference.

In the Five Dynasties period Emperor Taizu of Liang made Bianzhou his capital, calling it Dongdu, the Eastern Capital. It was the capital of the Later Liang (913 to 923), Later Jin (936 to 946), Later Han (947 to 950) and Later Zhou (951 to 960). The Song dynasty made Bian its capital when it overthrew the Later Zhou in 960, and named it the Eastern Capital, Dongjing.

After 1127 it became in 1130 the capital of a Han-ruled puppet kingdom called Great Qi, until 1138, and then came under the direct rule of the Jin. The Jin moved their court there in 1214. Under Mongol rule it was the capital of Henan Jiangbei Province, established in 1268. In 1368 the Ming captured it and restored the name Kaifeng. It remained the capital of Henan from the Ming into the early years of the People's Republic.
sections.life:
The Dongjing Menghualu, a nostalgic memoir of the city, describes the market outside Donghua Gate, where food, seasonal fruits and flowers, fish, jade and clothing were sold, and a customer who asked for a dozen dishes to go with wine would be served at once. Besides the day markets there were night markets and dawn markets. The main street was called the Imperial Street. Patrol stations stood every two or three hundred steps, and the patrolmen directed pedestrians and vehicles by day and guarded government offices and merchants' residences at night.

The city's restaurants, taverns and theatres could entertain thousands of people, with daily performances of storytelling, singing, puppet shows, dance and acrobatics. Zhang Zeduan's painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival shows the Bian River and its banks during the festival. The chrysanthemum was grown in Kaifeng for 1,600 years, and its cultivation reached its height under the Song, until the Jurchens took the city.

Under the Song the capital's government was the Kaifeng Prefecture, the only prefecture of the Capital Region. Su Song, an engineer, scientist and statesman, built a well-known astronomical clock tower, crowned with a rotating armillary sphere driven by water. From the 8th or 9th century until the 19th, Kaifeng had the oldest surviving Jewish community in China, the Kaifeng Jews. The city also has a significant Muslim enclave and a number of women's mosques, the oldest of which, the Wangjia Hutong Women's Mosque, dates to 1820.
sections.crises:
The city declined in the turmoil at the end of the Western Jin and in the Sixteen Kingdoms era. In 1127 it was occupied by the Jin. The Jin ruler ordered all its assets and its captives, including the Song imperial family and officials who refused to escape, to be taken to the Jin capital, Shangjing, near present-day Harbin. Prince Zhao Gou escaped and moved the remaining Song court away. The Jurchens withdrew during the year, but the Song court never returned, and they took the city again in 1130.

The Jin moved their own court to Kaifeng in 1214, relying on the line of the Yellow River against the Mongols. In 1233 the city fell to Mongol forces after a siege of ten months, and it was looted and all the Jin family members were killed. In 1358 and 1359 Red Turban rebels led by Liu Futong and Han Lin'er briefly held it, until they were crushed by Yuan forces.

The city lay on the Grand Canal but was militarily vulnerable on the floodplain of the Yellow River. Five major floods devastated it between 1375 and 1416, and there were more than 300 floods from the Southern Song to the late Qing. In 1410 a flood destroyed the city and killed 14,000 households. In 1642 rebels attacked Kaifeng three times, and in the third siege the Ming army flooded the city with the Yellow River to drown them. The whole city was submerged, and only 30,000 of its 370,000 people remained. It was abandoned, rebuilt in 1662, and rebuilt again in 1843 after the flood of 1841.
sections.legacy:
Kaifeng is one of the Eight Ancient Capitals of China, having been the capital eight times. The Iron Pagoda of the Youguo Temple, built in 1049 and 54.7 m high, survived war and floods and is the oldest landmark in the city. The Po Pagoda, dating from 974, was partly destroyed. The Daxiangguo Temple was built in 555.

Marco Polo arrived at Kaifeng in 1260 and wrote about it in his diaries. From June 1938 to August 1945 the Japanese Imperial Army occupied it. In 1948 the Battle of Kaifeng between Communist and Nationalist forces ended in a victory for the People's Liberation Army and the collapse of the Nationalist forces there. In October 1954 the capital of Henan was moved to Zhengzhou, and in September 1983 Kaifeng City was formed from former prefectures and districts.

Kaifeng cuisine plays a dominant part in forming Henan cuisine, and its night markets continue those of the Song. The chrysanthemum is the city flower. In 2020 the prefecture had 4,824,016 inhabitants, of whom 1,735,581 lived in the metropolitan area of five districts. It is a prefecture-level city of Henan province, with a campus of Henan University.

summary: Kaifeng, on the Yellow River in Henan, began as the Wei capital Daliang in 361 BCE. As the Song capital Dongjing it was probably the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127, and it was repeatedly taken and flooded, most destructively in 1642.
references: Arthur Cotterell, The Imperial Capitals of China: An Inside View of the Celestial Empire (Pimlico, 2007)
notes: No history article was given; only wp/kaifeng.txt used.
START: 361 BCE is the founding of Daliang by King Hui of Wei. The article also names two earlier Spring and Autumn cities, Yi and Qifeng, with no dates; the 'where' fact mentions them.

POPULATION of Dongjing: the article gives both 'over 400,000 living inside and outside the wall' and 'probably between 600,000 and 700,000' in the 11th century. I gave both, the second with its hedge in growth.
'Largest city in the world 1013 to 1127' is 'it is believed' in the article; hedged. 'Largest and most prosperous city in China' is stated flatly.

Dates of the Jin's first capture: the article says 1127, then again 1130. Chrysanthemum loss given as 'the Jürchens in 1126' in the Chrysanthemum section against 1127 elsewhere; I wrote only 'until the Jurchens took the city'.

Marco Polo in 1260: attributed to the article as written. Left unhedged only as 'according to the article on the city'; the editor may wish to drop it, as Marco Polo's visit is disputed in general (not in the article) and the phrase speaks of its source.
The Hongwu-era secondary Northern Capital designation (named Beijing, 1368 to 1378) left out for space; Kaifeng became capital of Henan province in 1378.
Ming: article says Kaifeng 'remained the capital of Henan from Ming to the early years of the People's Republic' and that the provincial capital moved in 1954.

Jewish community: article gives 'from the 8th to 9th century and up to the 19th century'; I wrote 'from the 8th or 9th century until the 19th'. The article says in the same sentence 'oldest extant' community; stated as 'oldest surviving'. The 2016 count left out as an 'as of' figure.
Name gloss ('opening the border', 'hidden', 'vengeance') left out as unclear.
The 1642 flooding: 'by the Ming army' as the article says; 'rebels' as the article says. The 1410 flood is 'killing 14,000 households' as given.
